main.title: Gran Turismo 2
main.summary: Gran Turismo 2 is a 1999 sim racing video game developed by Polyphony Digital and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Polyphony Digital’s PlayStation sequel
cards.text: Gran Turismo 2 is a 1999 sim racing video game developed by Polyphony Digital and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. It is the sequel to Gran Turismo, the second installment of the Gran Turismo series, and the first video game to be developed by Polyphony Digital.

cards.heading: A worldwide commercial success
cards.text: Gran Turismo 2 was a critical and commercial success, shipping 1.73 million units in Asia, 3.96 million units in North America, and 3.68 million units in Europe for a total of 9.37 million units as of April 30, 2008, and eventually becoming a Sony Greatest Hits game.

cards.heading: Arcade and Simulation modes
cards.text: Gran Turismo 2 is a racing simulation video game. The player must maneuver an automobile to compete against computer-controlled drivers on various race tracks. The game uses two different modes: Arcade Mode and Simulation Mode (Gran Turismo Mode in PAL and Japanese versions). In Arcade Mode, the player can freely choose vehicles they wish to use, and can enable damage, while Simulation Mode requires the player to earn driver's licenses, pay for vehicles, and earn trophies in order to unlock new and returning courses. Gran Turismo 2 features nearly 650 automobiles and 27 racing tracks, including rally tracks.

cards.heading: More cars, tracks and events
cards.text: Compared with Gran Turismo, the gameplay, physics and graphics are very similar: the only real noticeable difference in vehicle dynamics was the brakes, which became much less likely to lock up and cause the vehicle to oversteer. The major changes are the vastly expanded number of cars, tracks and races in Simulation Mode. Other differences include that the player can race events separately, if they do not want to enter the whole tournament. The player is no longer able to "qualify" for each race entered.

cards.heading: Expectations after the first game
cards.text: Following Gran Turismo's success, Polys Entertainment became Polyphony Digital. Kazunori Yamauchi set out to improve on the first game, while Sony's American marketing and sales teams expected strong holiday demand. Their public statements reflected the commercial momentum behind the sequel after the original's continued popularity.

cards.heading: Errors in the released version
cards.text: Players found errors after release, and SCEA offered replacements for affected copies. One problem could put an excessively powerful Vector M12 LM into the Trial Mountain endurance race despite its entry restriction. The completion counter also expected 223 events although only 219 were available, preventing the displayed percentage from reaching its intended maximum. Removed and region-specific events had left that discrepancy in the final data.

cards.heading: Acclaim alongside release problems
cards.text: Gran Turismo 2 received widespread critical acclaim, including a Famitsu score of 34 out of 40. NextGen's Dan Egger considered it an outstanding racing game while criticising the rushed production and release problems. Reviews could therefore recognise the sequel's expanded driving experience alongside the errors players encountered.

main.title: Harvest Moon: Back to Nature
main.summary: Harvest Moon: Back to Nature is a 1999 video game in the farm simulation series Story of Seasons developed by Victor Interactive Software and published outside of Japan by Natsume.

cards.text: Harvest Moon: Back to Nature is a 1999 video game in the farm simulation series Story of Seasons developed by Victor Interactive Software and published outside of Japan by Natsume. It is the first Harvest Moon game for a non-Nintendo console. Characters from Harvest Moon 64 were transferred to be the characters in this game, although with new lifestyles, personalities, and relatives.

A version featuring a female protagonist, Harvest Moon for Girl, was released in Japan on December 7, 2000. In 2005, Harvest Moon: Back to Nature was coupled and ported as Harvest Moon: Boy & Girl for the PlayStation Portable. In 2008, Marvelous Interactive released Harvest Moon: Back to Nature and Harvest Moon for Girl for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable via the PlayStation Network.

This game was remade as the Game Boy Advance games Harvest Moon: Friends of Mineral Town and Harvest Moon: More Friends of Mineral Town, both of which would later get a remake of their own for the Nintendo Switch under the name Story of Seasons: Friends of Mineral Town.

main.title: Space Channel 5
main.summary: Space Channel 5 is a 1999 music video game developed and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.

cards.text: Space Channel 5 is a 1999 music video game developed and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It was later ported to the PlayStation 2 and Game Boy Advance. Following space-faring reporter Ulala as she investigates an alien invasion, players engage in rhythm-based combat where Ulala mimics the actions of rivals in time to musical tracks.

The game was conceived by Tetsuya Mizuguchi, who was told to create something aimed at a female audience. Production lasted two years, with a staff of around 20 that included company veterans and newcomers to game development. The music, composed by Naofumi Hataya and Kenichi Tokoi, drew inspiration from big band music, including Ken Woodman's song "Mexican Flyer", which served as the game's theme song. The visual style was influenced by culture from the 1950s and 1960s and the later music videos of Peter Gabriel and Michael Jackson, the latter having a cameo appearance in the game.

While the game was released to low sales, it received generally positive reviews; praise focused on its music-based gameplay and art direction, but it was also faulted for its short length and syncing issues with the graphics. The PlayStation 2 version met with similar praise, with many recommending it due to the low selling price. The Game Boy Advance version, subtitled Ulala's Cosmic Attack, saw lower scores due to technical shortcomings. The game has since spawned a series of related games and media, beginning with the sequel Space Channel 5: Part 2, released in 2002 in Japan and 2003 worldwide.

main.title: Mario Party 2
main.subtitle: Another round in costume
main.summary: Mario Party 2 is Hudson Soft's 1999 Nintendo 64 board-game sequel for up to four players. Mario and his friends dress for themed lands, from pirates to space travellers. Turns on the board alternate with minigames, while collected Coins pay for Stars and items that can change the competition.

cards.heading: Another round in costume
cards.text: Mario Party 2 is Hudson Soft's 1999 Nintendo 64 board-game sequel for up to four players. Mario and his friends dress for themed lands, from pirates to space travellers. Turns on the board alternate with minigames, while collected Coins pay for Stars and items that can change the competition.

cards.heading: Spending for the next turn
cards.text: Reaching Toad with twenty Coins buys a Star, then moves the next opportunity elsewhere. Items offer ways to alter that journey, but each character can carry only one. A purchase therefore asks what the next turn needs most. A Magic Lamp goes straight to Toad, while other tools change movement or interfere with a rival's position.

cards.heading: Learning the land
cards.text: Each land gives the route its own complications. In Horror Land, day and night change the paths that the Whomps can block. Space Land counts down towards a Bowser Coin Beam that strips the Coins from anyone caught in its line. Learning the board means noticing these changes early enough to weigh another route before the die decides how far the character travels.

cards.heading: A contest inside the contest
cards.text: A minigame follows once every player has moved, with the spaces they occupy helping decide the teams. Earnings return to the board and make the next purchase possible. Bonus Stars can also reward the strongest minigame performance or other accomplishments at the end. The final result therefore draws together many short contests, including turns whose importance was less obvious when they happened.

main.title: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium
main.subtitle: A crossover that fits in a pocket
main.summary: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium is SNK's portable crossover fighter, released for Neo Geo Pocket Color in December 1999.

cards.heading: A crossover that fits in a pocket
cards.text: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium is SNK's portable crossover fighter, released for Neo Geo Pocket Color in December 1999. Characters from the two companies meet in a compact, animated style, bringing their recognizable attacks to a handheld contest. The player can choose a single fighter, a two-person tag team or a three-person team. Those formats make the same roster useful in different ways, from mastering one character to deciding how several fighters should share the course of a match.

cards.heading: Choose the team and the fighting system
cards.text: The choice of gauge system adds another layer. Average mode follows a Capcom-style level meter, Counter uses an SNK-style charge gauge, and Rush strengthens super attacks when its meter fills. That decision changes how a fighter builds towards a powerful move. Rival encounters interrupt the tournament, while the final opponents connect the chosen character to the opposing company's world. Reaching the full ending also opens a character-unlocking sequence, giving the single-player journey another reward beyond simply winning the last ordinary fight.

cards.heading: A festival beyond the main tournament
cards.text: Olympic mode turns the crossover into a broader collection of challenges, including survival and time-attack events alongside minigames inspired by Metal Slug and Ghosts 'n Goblins. Performance earns Versus points that can unlock special attacks. Link features also connect the cartridge to other compatible games, including Dreamcast releases. The small device becomes a meeting place for several arcade traditions, combining a carefully structured fighting game with playful references to the characters and genres surrounding it. Later reissues brought the handheld original to Switch and Windows.

main.title: Valkyrie Profile
main.subtitle: Fallen warriors, timed battles
main.summary: On December 22, 1999, tri-Ace released Valkyrie Profile for PlayStation in Japan.

cards.heading: Warriors for Ragnarok
cards.text: Released in Japan on December 22, 1999, tri-Ace's Valkyrie Profile puts the player in charge of Lenneth, a Valkyrie gathering fallen warriors for Ragnarok. Its PlayStation adventure combines side-scrolling exploration with party battles controlled through the face buttons. Time is divided into periods: visiting a location or developing a recruit uses part of the schedule, giving the divine assignment a practical deadline.

cards.heading: Lives before the party
cards.text: Many future party members appear first in scenes leading to their deaths. Relationships, ambitions and misfortunes introduce each warrior before Lenneth recruits their soul as an Einherjar. These short stories give the party a history beyond its combat statistics. People from different circumstances meet again under Lenneth's command, preparing for a war whose demands reach far beyond their former lives.

cards.heading: Four fighters, four buttons
cards.text: Each active fighter is assigned to a face button. The player combines their attacks into sequences, judging when a strike will launch an enemy or keep it airborne. Different attack rhythms make the order of inputs important: a useful combination depends on the interaction between characters as well as their individual strength. Chaining blows also builds towards special attacks.

cards.heading: Memories beyond the assignment
cards.text: Multiple endings depend on the player's actions and choices. Preparing warriors for Asgard follows Lenneth's official duty, while investigating memories and relationships can reveal more about her own identity. With limited periods available, the search for those connections must fit around exploration and training. The structure gives players reasons to reconsider both their route through the world and the orders they have been following.

main.title: D2
main.subtitle: Laura in the snow
main.summary: D2 is Warp's survival horror adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 23 December 1999.

cards.heading: Laura in the snow
cards.text: D2 is Warp's survival horror adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 23 December 1999. Directed by Kenji Eno, it places Laura in the Canadian wilderness after an air disaster, with isolated buildings and creatures interrupting the snow-covered journey. Laura had appeared as the central figure of D, but this game gives her an independent story and a more action-oriented structure. Outdoor exploration uses a third-person view, while interiors shift to first person, changing the player's relationship to the spaces as the journey moves between exposure and shelter.

cards.heading: Surviving between encounters
cards.text: Monsters interrupt outdoor exploration in random encounters. Laura remains in place during these fights, so the player aims and fires rather than running around the enemy. Victories earn experience and increase her health capacity. A submachine gun supplies unlimited ammunition, while a hunting rifle is used to kill animals for meat that restores health. Hunting therefore connects the landscape to survival between the stranger confrontations. The change between walking, aiming and searching gives the wilderness several purposes, with each interruption asking for a different kind of attention.

cards.heading: A quieter way to observe
cards.text: Laura also carries a camera, allowing pictures to be taken outside cinematic sequences and saved to a VMU for later viewing. That option creates a quieter activity within an otherwise threatening journey, encouraging the player to stop and look at the surroundings. Eno also composed the music, connecting the game's visual and sonic direction. D2 combines these different tempos within the same isolated setting: an outdoor journey may pause for a photograph or a hunt, then be interrupted by an encounter in which movement gives way entirely to aiming.

main.title: Shenmue
main.subtitle: Life goes on even while you wait
main.summary: On December 29, 1999, SEGA released Shenmue: Chapter 1 Yokosuka for Dreamcast in Japan.

cards.heading: An investigation in everyday time
cards.text: SEGA released Shenmue: Chapter 1 Yokosuka for Dreamcast in Japan on December 29, 1999. Yu Suzuki's adventure follows Ryo's search for his father's killer through a town organised around everyday routines. Shops open and close, residents move between appointments, and weather changes as the days pass. Investigation shares the streets with martial-arts training, arcade games, collectibles and sudden action sequences.

cards.heading: Learning the town's schedule
cards.text: The Time Control system makes the hour matter during an investigation. A shop may be closed or a witness elsewhere; an appointment can require Ryo to return later. Looking for information means learning these schedules and deciding how to use the intervals between them. Familiar streets take on different uses as the day advances, and a previous unsuccessful visit can suggest when to try again.

cards.heading: Finding people through their routines
cards.text: The fully voiced residents follow routines that carry them between work, home and other places. Asking questions gradually builds a picture of who knows the neighbourhood and where someone might be found. The investigation depends on those everyday connections. Repeated encounters also make residents familiar, giving Ryo's route through Yokosuka a social geography as well as a physical one.

cards.heading: A changing sky over familiar streets
cards.text: Magic Weather changes atmospheric conditions with the internal calendar. Rain, snow and different skies vary streets that Ryo crosses repeatedly during the investigation. This gives the passing days a visible presence without requiring a succession of new locations. Dobuita remains recognisable while its appearance changes around the player's routines.

cards.heading: A sudden prompt for action
cards.text: Quick Time Events interrupt exploration with contextual prompts during chases and other directed action scenes. Players react quickly to keep a sequence moving while the camera follows a planned course. Alongside free combat, this gives Shenmue several ways to handle action. A quiet exchange can suddenly demand a dodge or pursuit, producing a sharp change from the pace of the investigation.

cards.heading: Time at the arcade
cards.text: Arcades, capsule toys and training offer ways to spend time between leads. Ryo can leave the investigation for a SEGA arcade game or another small activity, making the town useful beyond the next story objective. These diversions also place arcade culture inside Yokosuka's everyday life. Deciding when to return to the search becomes part of finding a personal routine within the town.

cards.heading: From Saturn to Dreamcast
cards.text: Suzuki's GDC postmortem traces the project through an early connection to Virtua Fighter and development on Sega Saturn before its move to Dreamcast. Its ambitions required large amounts of character, animation and environmental data, together with systems that responded to time. The long production joined SEGA's experience in three-dimensional fighting games to a different problem: making everyday movement through a town sustain an adventure.

main.title: Banjo-Tooie
main.subtitle: A partnership that can split in two
main.summary: Rare’s 2000 Nintendo 64 sequel expands the bear and bird’s adventure into eight worlds, with new abilities, transformations and occasions when the partners must work apart.

cards.heading: Beyond Spiral Mountain
cards.text: Released in 2000 for Nintendo 64, Banjo-Tooie continues Rare’s partnership between Banjo the bear and Kazooie the bird. Gruntilda returns, and the adventure reaches eight worlds beyond Spiral Mountain. Jigsaw pieces open the way forward, while musical notes help the pair learn new abilities from Jamjars. Exploration involves remembering a place, recognising what is missing and returning with a move that changes what can be done there.

cards.heading: Together, apart, together again
cards.text: The partnership itself becomes a puzzle tool: Banjo and Kazooie can separate and use their own abilities before joining forces again. Mumbo Jumbo can also be controlled, while Humba Wumba transforms Banjo into different forms. These changes give familiar spaces new uses. Alongside the main adventure, competitive minigames support two to four players. Grant Kirkhope’s music accompanies a sequel built around expanding the possibilities of characters the player already knows.

main.title: Bugs Bunny & Taz: Time Busters
main.subtitle: Two ways to cause trouble
main.summary: A rabbit’s ingenuity and a spinning whirlwind turn a broken time machine into a partnership.

cards.heading: A clock out of joint
cards.text: Released in 2000 for PlayStation and Windows, Bugs Bunny & Taz: Time Busters is Artificial Mind & Movement’s return to the Looney Tunes world after Bugs Bunny: Lost in Time. When Daffy Duck disrupts Granny’s Time Regulator, Bugs and Taz must recover the Time Gem across Aztec, Viking, Arabian and Transylvanian settings. The historical costumes give their cartoon tricks a new setting in each period.

cards.heading: A double act you can play
cards.text: The pair’s different abilities are the central idea. Bugs can investigate rabbit holes and handle obstacles with his own tricks; Taz spins through trouble and supplies the strength that Bugs lacks. Switching characters turns a familiar platform adventure into a sequence of shared tasks, while the PlayStation version also supports two-player cooperation. Their quarrels become a working relationship. Gilles Léveillé and Studio Global are credited with the original music.
